assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks at the 10^-18 level are a clear case of progress limited by what can be measured and how accurately. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice concept, with strontium and ytterbium clocks, removed the Doppler and recoil problem while keeping a large atom number, and it enabled a leap in stability with consequences for geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and a possible redefinition of the second.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and Ye drove the experimental accuracy and stability records, so a two-person prize is a natural configuration. Other groups (e.g. ion-clock and lattice-clock efforts elsewhere) contributed, but the decisive concept plus precision demonstration sits with these two to the best of my knowledge.
assessment.maturity: Independent confirmation across many laboratories at 10^-18 is established, and comparison between clocks is routine. Recognition appears timely and not premature; the formal redefinition of the second is still pending but does not affect the discovery.
uncertainties: Whether the committee wishes to separate the lattice-clock concept from the broader frequency-comb and clock lineage that was already recognised earlier.
I have not independently verified priority details among the lattice-clock contributors.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation with ultracold atoms in optical lattices turned the Bose-Hubbard and Fermi-Hubbard models into controllable laboratory systems, with the superfluid to Mott-insulator transition, single-site imaging and strongly correlated many-body dynamics. It is a broad, lasting platform that connects atomic physics to condensed-matter questions.
assessment.attribution: The theoretical proposal for the Mott transition and lattice quantum simulation (Zoller and Cirac with collaborators) and the experimental realisations (Greiner, Bloch, Esslinger) are separable. Five names are credited, so a choice among them is needed; I select a theory-plus-experiment pairing, but excluding Cirac and Esslinger is a real attribution cost.
assessment.maturity: Mature and heavily confirmed over two decades, with many independent groups. Recognition is timely; part of the surrounding field (laser cooling, BEC) has already been honoured.
uncertainties: Allocation among five credited names is unresolved and any three leave out well-deserving contributors.
Overlap with the trapped-ion and Rydberg quantum-simulation candidates may split the case.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The theoretical prediction of flat bands at the magic angle and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in twisted bilayer graphene opened moire quantum matter as a major new field with rapid and wide impact.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the key theoretical prediction; Jarillo-Herrero's group made the decisive experimental discovery. This is a clean three-person theory plus experiment configuration. Other experimental groups (e.g. Dean, Young, Yazdani, Efetov) contributed later results and are not in the credited names.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed independently by many groups, though the field is young and some interpretation of the superconducting mechanism remains open. Possibly slightly early but the basic discovery is well established.
uncertainties: The mechanism of superconductivity in the magic-angle system is not settled.
Credit for the experimental discovery may extend beyond the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Programmable arrays of optical-tweezer-trapped neutral atoms with Rydberg-mediated entanglement have become a leading platform for quantum simulation and computation, building on single-atom trapping and Rydberg blockade ideas. The work is technically elegant and has produced new many-body states and high-fidelity gates.
assessment.attribution: Saffman contributed early Rydberg-gate proposals and later experiments, Browaeys demonstrated single-atom tweezer arrays and Rydberg blockade, and Lukin's group scaled programmable arrays; the Rydberg gate theory (Jaksch, Cirac, Zoller and others) is not in the credited names, which complicates attribution.
assessment.maturity: Rapidly maturing, with independent groups reproducing key results, but the field is still moving and the long-term significance for scalable computation is not yet clear. Likely somewhat early.
uncertainties: Priority among tweezer-array, Rydberg-blockade and gate-proposal contributions is not clean.
Lukin appears in several candidates (B004, B021, B054) and the committee should avoid double counting.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators and the experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells founded a large area of topological quantum matter with conceptual depth and lasting impact on materials physics.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical prediction, and Molenkamp's group did the first experimental realisation (with the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal in the background, not in the credited names). The configuration is reasonably clear but the BHZ and 3D topological insulator contributions are unresolved.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by independent experiments; however the topological-phases theme was recognised in 2016, so the committee should judge whether this is a distinct discovery.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2016 prize on topological phase transitions.
Omitted contributors such as Bernevig, Zhang and the 3D topological insulator discoverers.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum interfaces between light and matter, covering cavity QED, electromagnetically induced transparency and atomic-ensemble memories, underpin quantum memories and networks. My own work on rare-earth-ion crystal memories lies in this area, so I rank it below its intrinsic standing to avoid favouring my own field; the scientific idea is sound and important.
assessment.attribution: Credit is spread across many approaches (single-atom cavity systems, atomic ensembles, solid-state memories). Kimble, Rempe and Lukin are leading figures, but a three-person prize cannot represent the full set, and my own colleagues and I are not in the credited names.
assessment.maturity: Experimental demonstrations are numerous and independent, but quantum networks are still at an early stage, so recognition may be premature relative to technological payoff.
uncertainties: Compound topic with different platforms that may merit different recognition.
Potential bias from my own research area in quantum memories.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry provides inertial, gravitational and fundamental-constant measurements at high precision and tests of the equivalence principle, with a direct link to precision sensing.
assessment.attribution: Bordé proposed early atomic interferometer concepts, Pritchard demonstrated the first atom interferometers with gratings, and Kasevich built precision gravimeters and gyroscopes with Raman pulses; the credit with Chu and others is somewhat entangled with the laser-cooling prize.
assessment.maturity: Mature and widely used, though application to fundamental tests still has uncertain discovery-level outcomes. Recognition would be timely.
uncertainties: Credit overlaps with Chu and Cohen-Tannoudji lineage.
Whether the case is for a discovery or for a measurement technique.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light for quantum-enhanced interferometry combines a clear theoretical proposal with laboratory demonstration and its use in gravitational-wave detectors, so the quantum noise limit on measurement was beaten in practice.
assessment.attribution: Caves provided the 1981 proposal, Kimble and colleagues the early experimental squeezing, and Schnabel and Mavalvala the application to detectors; Mavalvala is also credited, so choosing three leaves out someone important.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by routine use at LIGO and GEO600, so mature; however the 2017 prize already recognised gravitational-wave detection, which the committee may regard as covering part of the impact.
uncertainties: Four credited names for a three-person limit.
